chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:

Sadaqat al-fitrah is upon every head among your household: the young and the old, the free and the slave, the rich and the poor. For every person there is half a sa' of wheat or barley, or one sa' of dates or raisins, for the poor among the Muslims. And he said: Dates are more beloved to me.

Thus, the proper approach regarding these hadiths and others of their kind is that we interpret them as indicating a kind of recommendation, not obligation and requirement, because the obligation pertains to one who is wealthy, the least state of which is that he possesses the amount upon which zakat becomes obligatory. Whoever is not like that is encouraged to give the zakat from what he receives and what is given in charity to him, but that is not obligatory, as we have explained, and what follows further clarifies that.

key_terms.صَاعٌ: a full sa' as the prescribed measure for dates or raisins
key_terms.صَدَقَةُ ٱلْفِطْرَةِ: the alms of fitrah given at the end of Ramadan
key_terms.فُقَرَاءِ ٱلْمُسْلِمِينَ: the poor among the Muslims who are recipients
key_terms.كُلِّ رَأْسٍ: every individual person under one's responsibility
key_terms.نِصْفُ صَاعٍ: half a sa' as the prescribed measure for some food types
key_terms.ٱلزَّكَاةُ: the obligatory alms used here as the qualifying financial threshold

ai.seo_question: Is sadaqat al-fitrah obligatory upon a poor person in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This report discusses the ruling of sadaqat al-fitrah for members of one's household and mentions the standard measures of staple foods to be given to the poor among the Muslims. The concluding legal clarification explains that reports mentioning the poor are to be understood as recommending payment from them, while the actual obligation applies to the wealthy person who possesses the qualifying amount.
